topicTitle: Semiconductors — intrinsic and extrinsic, p-n junction, diode, transistor
notes: An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure crystal. At room temperature a few bonds break, giving equal numbers of free electrons and holes. Heating frees more pairs, so the conductivity rises.

An extrinsic semiconductor has been doped. A group-15 atom adds a spare electron and makes n-type material, in which electrons are the majority carriers. A group-13 atom leaves a hole and makes p-type material.
The doped crystal is still electrically neutral. The extra carriers come with the atom's nuclear charge. n-type does not mean the lump of silicon is negative.

A p-n junction has a depletion layer. Forward bias, with the p-side positive, lowers the barrier and current flows. Silicon needs about 0.7 V before that current becomes large. Reverse bias widens the barrier and only a leakage current flows.
A bipolar transistor has emitter, base and collector. A small base current controls a much larger collector current. The current gain β is I_c / I_b.
An LED is a forward-biased junction that emits light when electrons and holes recombine. A photodiode is used the other way: light creates pairs and a reverse current.

summary: A pure semiconductor has equal electrons and holes. Doping makes n-type material, with electron majority carriers, or p-type material, with hole majority carriers. A junction conducts when the p-side is positive. In a transistor, β = I_c / I_b, so a small base current controls a larger collector current.
